appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Bontemps lets slip the Buttes-Chaumont habit and Andrée's telegram of 15 September; the narrator concludes: Alors Albertine l'attendait à Balbec et me l'avait caché, and rereads her tender words as le reflet d'un changement intervenu dans une situation que nous ne connaissons pas, celui de la variation de la conduite des femmes qui ne nous aiment pas.
appraisal_events.explanation: An outsider's casual testimony retroactively convicts Albertine of lying (she had denied ever going to the Buttes-Chaumont) and strips her earlier sacrifice of its generous motive, so the passage locally reevaluates her as deceitful and indifferent rather than devoted.

appraisal_events.evidence: Je ne voulais pas qu'Albertine pût me mépriser comme ayant été dupe d'elle et d'Andrée; ma vie avec Albertine n'était, pour une part, quand je n'étais pas jaloux, qu'ennui, pour l'autre part, quand j'étais jaloux, que souffrance; and the closing outburst, criai-je de toutes mes forces, hors de moi, immediately undercut by Albertine's mocking lines from Esther on his ce front irrité.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrating voice steadily lowers its own past self: dupe of the two women, jailer who cannot speak for fear of losing his prisoner, reduced to boredom or torment, and finally to a shouted reproach that the recalled Esther quotation turns into a spectacle of ridiculous rage.

status_effects.explanation: She is locally devalued as a liar whose apparent devotion is exposed as the convenient by-product of a private assignation.

Her secrecy gives her leverage: the narrator dares not confront her, keeps buying Fortuny dresses, and calibrates the moment of rupture around her possible departure, while she qui ne m'en savait aucun gré.
He ends the passage as the losing party: duped, jealous, unable to travel or to speak frankly, and humiliated by his own uncontrolled anger.

ambiguities: Only the Buttes-Chaumont contradiction and the telegram are attested from outside; the erotic reconstruction (the empty apartment of Andrée's grandmother, the complicit valet) is the jealous narrator's own imagining, and the passage explicitly offers a consoling counter-reading (Albertine's habit of making one action serve several people) before discarding it, so the strength of the blame against Albertine is partly self-generated.

Andrée is materially implicated as the suspected lover but is never independently evaluated; her diminishment exists only inside the narrator's suspicion, so no separate status effect is recorded for her.
